ar: عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم قَالَ: «لَوْ يُعْطَى النَّاسُ بِدَعْوَاهُمْ لَادَّعَى رِجَالٌ أَمْوَالَ قَوْمٍ وَدِمَاءَهُمْ، لَكِنَّ الْبَيِّنَةَ عَلَى الْمُدَّعِي، وَالْيَمِينَ عَلَى مَنْ أَنْكَرَ».

s: Al-Bayhaqi and others report this from Ibn ‘Abbas, and an-Nawawi calls it hasan; its first part is in al-Bukhari and Muslim: “If people were given what they claim, men would claim the wealth and blood of others.” The rule of evidence that follows is that the claimant brings proof, and the oath is on the one who denies.
m: A court cannot decide on assertions. If a claim were enough, the strong and the shameless would take what they wanted: a man might say that another owes him money, or that he has a right to his land. The Prophet ﷺ makes proof the claimant’s task. This protects the weak and the absent, and it makes the court a place of evidence, not of power.

Most jurists see this as one of the foundations of Islamic procedure: the presumption of innocence and the burden on the claimant. The oath is not a punishment but a means of ending a dispute when there is no proof.
l: Do not accuse without proof, in the court or in conversation.
Be honest in testimony and in claims.
Protect the rights of others, even when they are not there to defend themselves.

en: On the authority of Ibn ‘Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “If people were given whatever they claimed, men would claim the wealth and lives of others. But the burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies.”

ar: عَنْ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ الْخُدْرِيّ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ سَمِعْت رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم يَقُولُ: مَنْ رَأَى مِنْكُمْ مُنْكَرًا فَلْيُغَيِّرْهُ بِيَدِهِ، فَإِنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ فَبِلِسَانِهِ، فَإِنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ فَبِقَلْبِهِ، وَذَلِكَ أَضْعَفُ الْإِيمَانِ.

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri, and the occasion is a famous scene. On a day of Eid in Madinah, Marwan ibn al-Hakam, the governor, went up to the pulpit and began the sermon before the prayer, which was contrary to the Prophet’s practice, in which the prayer came first. A man stood up and said, “The prayer comes before the sermon.” Marwan said, “That has been left.” Abu Sa‘id said, “This man has done his duty. I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say...”
m: “Whoever of you sees something wrong, let him change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart, and that is the weakest of faith.” Three levels, depending on capacity and authority. The hand: for the one who has the power and the right, such as a parent in the home or an official in his office, and in a way that does not lead to a greater harm. The tongue: advice, speaking, teaching. The heart: to hate the wrong and refuse to accept it.

Scholars add conditions: the person must know that the thing is wrong, must not cause something worse, and must act with kindness. The Qur’an says to call with wisdom and good counsel (16:125). The last level, the heart, is always possible, and is the least of faith. It does not mean that a person is excused from all effort when he has any means.
l: When you see a wrong, ask what you can actually do at your level, and do it with wisdom.
Advise privately and gently, since it leaves the person their dignity.
Do not let your heart become used to what is wrong.

en: On the authority of Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; and if he cannot, then with his heart, and that is the weakest of faith.”

ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم لَا تَحَاسَدُوا، وَلَا تَنَاجَشُوا، وَلَا تَبَاغَضُوا، وَلَا تَدَابَرُوا، وَلَا يَبِعْ بَعْضُكُمْ عَلَى بَيْعِ بَعْضٍ، وَكُونُوا عِبَادَ اللَّهِ إخْوَانًا، الْمُسْلِمُ أَخُو الْمُسْلِمِ، لَا يَظْلِمُهُ، وَلَا يَخْذُلُهُ، وَلَا يَكْذِبُهُ، وَلَا يَحْقِرُهُ، التَّقْوَى هَاهُنَا، وَيُشِيرُ إلَى صَدْرِهِ ثَلَاثَ مَرَّاتٍ، بِحَسْبِ امْرِئٍ مِنْ الشَّرِّ أَنْ يَحْقِرَ أَخَاهُ الْمُسْلِمَ، كُلُّ الْمُسْلِمِ عَلَى الْمُسْلِمِ حَرَامٌ: دَمُهُ وَمَالُهُ وَعِرْضُهُ.

s: Muslim reports this from Abu Hurayrah. It is a full summary of the ethics of brotherhood, a run of prohibitions followed by the rights of one Muslim over another. In the course of it the Prophet ﷺ points to his chest three times and says, “Taqwa is here.”
m: Do not envy one another (tahasadu). Do not artificially inflate prices to deceive (tanajashu). Do not hate one another. Do not turn your backs on one another. Do not undercut each other’s bargains. And be servants of Allah, brothers. Then the rights: a Muslim is the brother of a Muslim, so he does not wrong him, does not abandon him, does not lie to him and does not despise him. “It is enough evil for a man that he despises his brother Muslim.”

Then the sentence that grounds it all: “Every Muslim’s blood, wealth and honour are sacred to every Muslim.” Scholars note that honour (‘ird) is placed alongside blood and wealth, so backbiting and slander are a violation as real as theft. The place of taqwa is the heart, which is why no one can judge another’s piety by appearance, and why contempt is the sign of its absence.
l: Check your heart for envy and root it out with du‘a for the person.
Do not look down on anyone, whatever their situation.
Guard the honour of the absent as you guard their wealth.

en: On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Do not envy one another; do not inflate prices against one another; do not hate one another; do not turn away from one another; and do not undercut one another’s trade. Be servants of Allah, brothers. A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim: he does not wrong him, does not abandon him, does not lie to him and does not look down on him. Taqwa is here,” and he pointed to his chest three times. “It is evil enough for a person that he looks down on his Muslim brother. Every Muslim is sacred to every other Muslim: his blood, his property and his honour.”

ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه و سلم قَالَ: مَنْ نَفَّسَ عَنْ مُؤْمِنٍ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ الدُّنْيَا نَفَّسَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ، وَمَنْ يَسَّرَ عَلَى مُعْسِرٍ، يَسَّرَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ، وَمَنْ سَتَرَ مُسْلِما سَتَرَهُ اللهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ، وَاَللَّهُ فِي عَوْنِ الْعَبْدِ مَا كَانَ الْعَبْدُ فِي عَوْنِ أَخِيهِ، وَمَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا سَهَّلَ اللَّهُ لَهُ بِهِ طَرِيقًا إلَى الْجَنَّةِ، وَمَا اجْتَمَعَ قَوْمٌ فِي بَيْتٍ مِنْ بُيُوتِ اللَّهِ يَتْلُونَ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ، وَيَتَدَارَسُونَهُ فِيمَا بَيْنَهُمْ؛ إلَّا نَزَلَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ السَّكِينَةُ، وَغَشِيَتْهُمْ الرَّحْمَةُ، وَ حَفَّتهُمُ المَلاَئِكَة، وَذَكَرَهُمْ اللَّهُ فِيمَنْ عِنْدَهُ، وَمَنْ أَبَطْأَ بِهِ عَمَلُهُ لَمْ يُسْرِعْ بِهِ نَسَبُهُ.

s: Muslim reports this long hadith from Abu Hurayrah. It is the same as the hadith “A path to Paradise” in the library, and an-Nawawi includes it for its rich range of subjects: relief of hardship, concealing faults, helping, seeking knowledge, and the gatherings of Qur’an.
m: Notice the final lines, which are easy to miss. The Prophet ﷺ says that no people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it among themselves, but tranquillity (sakinah) descends on them, mercy covers them, the angels surround them, and Allah mentions them to those with Him. And then the closing sentence: “Whoever is slowed by his deeds, his lineage will not speed him.”

That final line puts the whole teaching in its right place. Family, rank and background do not carry the weight at the end. Deeds do. A person cannot rely on a name when his actions have lagged behind.
l: Join a circle of Qur’an or study regularly, and bring someone with you.
Do not rely on your family’s reputation for your standing with Allah.
Choose today one hardship to relieve for someone.

en:
On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Whoever relieves a believer of a hardship of this world, Allah will relieve him of a hardship of the Day of Resurrection. Whoever eases the way for one in difficulty, Allah will ease things for him in this world and the next. Whoever conceals the faults of a Muslim, Allah will conceal his faults in this world and the next. Allah is helping His servant as long as the servant is helping his brother.

Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise. No people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it among themselves, except that tranquillity descends on them, mercy covers them, the angels surround them, and Allah mentions them among those with Him. And whoever is slowed by his deeds will not be sped up by his lineage.”

ar: عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم فِيمَا يَرْوِيهِ عَنْ رَبِّهِ تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى، قَالَ: «إنَّ اللَّهَ كَتَبَ الْحَسَنَاتِ وَالسَّيِّئَاتِ، ثُمَّ بَيَّنَ ذَلِكَ، فَمَنْ هَمَّ بِحَسَنَةٍ فَلَمْ يَعْمَلْهَا كَتَبَهَا اللَّهُ عِنْدَهُ حَسَنَةً كَامِلَةً، وَإِنْ هَمَّ بِهَا فَعَمِلَهَا كَتَبَهَا اللَّهُ عِنْدَهُ عَشْرَ حَسَنَاتٍ إلَى سَبْعِمِائَةِ ضِعْفٍ إلَى أَضْعَافٍ كَثِيرَةٍ، وَإِنْ هَمَّ بِسَيِّئَةٍ فَلَمْ يَعْمَلْهَا كَتَبَهَا اللَّهُ عِنْدَهُ حَسَنَةً كَامِلَةً، وَإِنْ هَمَّ بِهَا فَعَمِلَهَا كَتَبَهَا اللَّهُ سَيِّئَةً وَاحِدَةً».

s: Al-Bukhari and Muslim report this from Ibn ‘Abbas as a hadith qudsi: the Prophet ﷺ relates from his Lord. It is among the clearest texts on the generosity of Allah’s accounting.
m: “Whoever intends a good deed and does not do it, Allah writes it with Himself as a complete good deed.” An intention that was sincere, but was prevented by a cause beyond the person’s control, is counted. “If he intends it and does it, Allah writes it as ten good deeds, up to seven hundred times, up to many times more.” The multiplication depends on sincerity, the benefit of the act, and its difficulty.

Then the other side: “Whoever intends an evil deed and does not do it, Allah writes it as a complete good deed. If he intends it and does it, Allah writes it as one evil deed.” Scholars explain that the one who intends evil and then leaves it for Allah’s sake receives a reward. If he leaves it because he was unable, or from other reasons, then there is no reward, as another hadith says. And the evil is recorded as one, not multiplied.
l: Make good intentions often. They are counted even if circumstances prevent you.
When you feel the pull to sin and you turn away for Allah’s sake, know that it is written as a good deed.
Take the multiplied reward seriously, and use time and effort for what has most benefit.

en: On the authority of Ibn ‘Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in what he relates from his Lord, the Blessed and Exalted, that He said: “Truly Allah has written down the good deeds and the bad deeds, and then He made that clear. So whoever intends a good deed and does not do it, Allah writes it with Himself as a complete good deed; and if he intends it and does it, Allah writes it with Himself as ten good deeds, up to seven hundred times, up to many times more. And whoever intends a bad deed and does not do it, Allah writes it with Himself as a complete good deed; and if he intends it and does it, Allah writes it as one bad deed.”

ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَة رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُول اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم إنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى قَالَ: مَنْ عَادَى لِي وَلِيًّا فَقْد آذَنْتهُ بِالْحَرْبِ، وَمَا تَقَرَّبَ إلَيَّ عَبْدِي بِشَيْءٍ أَحَبَّ إلَيَّ مِمَّا افْتَرَضْتُهُ عَلَيْهِ، وَلَا يَزَالُ عَبْدِي يَتَقَرَّبُ إلَيَّ بِالنَّوَافِلِ حَتَّى أُحِبَّهُ، فَإِذَا أَحْبَبْتُهُ كُنْت سَمْعَهُ الَّذِي يَسْمَعُ بِهِ، وَبَصَرَهُ الَّذِي يُبْصِرُ بِهِ، وَيَدَهُ الَّتِي يَبْطِشُ بِهَا، وَرِجْلَهُ الَّتِي يَمْشِي بِهَا، وَلَئِنْ سَأَلَنِي لَأُعْطِيَنَّهُ، وَلَئِنْ اسْتَعَاذَنِي لَأُعِيذَنَّهُ.

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from Abu Hurayrah as a hadith qudsi. It is the hadith of the awliya’, the friends of Allah, and a text that has been much discussed because of its wording about hearing and seeing, which the scholars explain with care.
m: It begins with a stern warning: “Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war on him.” Then it explains how one becomes close. “My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. And My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him.” The path: the obligatory first, then the voluntary on top of it.

“When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks.” Scholars of Ahl as-Sunnah explain that this does not mean that Allah is identical with a servant, or dwells in him. They say it means that the servant’s hearing, sight, hand and foot are guided and guarded by Allah, so that he hears only what pleases Allah and sees only what He permits; or that Allah grants him help in these faculties. “If he asks Me, I will give him; if he seeks refuge in Me, I will protect him.”

The last lines use the language of tenderness: “I hesitate in nothing I do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death and I dislike to harm him.” The scholars explain this as an expression of care, without implying any lack of knowledge on Allah’s part.
l: Build on the obligatory first and make it excellent. Then add voluntary prayer, fasting and charity.
Respect the people of Allah and do not wrong them.
Ask Him and seek refuge in Him: He has promised to give and to protect.

en: On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Truly Allah the Exalted said: Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war on him. My servant draws near to Me with nothing more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely protect him.”

ar: عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم قَالَ: «إنَّ اللَّهَ تَجَاوَزَ لِي عَنْ أُمَّتِي الْخَطَأَ وَالنِّسْيَانَ وَمَا اسْتُكْرِهُوا عَلَيْهِ».

s: Ibn Majah, al-Bayhaqi and others report this from Ibn ‘Abbas, and an-Nawawi calls it hasan. Some scholars discussed its chain, but its meaning is supported by the Qur’an: “Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we have forgotten or erred” (2:286), and the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah answered, “I have done so” (Muslim).
m: Three things are lifted from the community: error (khata’), forgetfulness (nisyan) and what a person is forced to do (ma istukrihu ‘alayh). It is a great relief. One who eats during Ramadan having forgotten that he was fasting has no sin and his fast is valid. One who is forced to say something under real threat is not held to the words, as the Qur’an says in the case of ‘Ammar ibn Yasir and the verse about the one who was compelled while his heart remained at rest in belief (16:106).

Scholars note that what is lifted is the sin. Obligations to people remain: if someone destroys another’s property by mistake, he must still compensate. The hadith is about accountability before Allah, and it shows the ease of the law.
l: When you realise you have erred or forgotten, correct what you can, ask forgiveness and move on.
Be gentle with the mistakes of others.
Remember the ease of this religion when scruples rise.

en: On the authority of Ibn ‘Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Truly Allah has pardoned for me my nation their mistakes, their forgetfulness, and what they are forced to do.”

ar: عَنْ ابْن عُمَرَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: أَخَذَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم بِمَنْكِبِي، وَقَالَ: كُنْ فِي الدُّنْيَا كَأَنَّك غَرِيبٌ أَوْ عَابِرُ سَبِيلٍ. وَكَانَ ابْنُ عُمَرَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا يَقُولُ: إذَا أَمْسَيْتَ فَلَا تَنْتَظِرْ الصَّبَاحَ، وَإِذَا أَصْبَحْتَ فَلَا تَنْتَظِرْ الْمَسَاءَ، وَخُذْ مِنْ صِحَّتِك لِمَرَضِك، وَمِنْ حَيَاتِك لِمَوْتِك.

s: Al-Bukhari reports this from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar, who said: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of my shoulder and said, ‘Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a wayfarer.’” The physical gesture is part of the lesson: it was a moment of personal attention. Ibn ‘Umar was a young man at the time.
m: A stranger in a foreign land does not build, does not settle, does not expect honour, and keeps his eyes on home. A wayfarer is even lighter: he carries only what he needs. The Prophet ﷺ is describing how to hold the world: use it, pass through it, and do not mistake it for a home.

Ibn ‘Umar used to add: “When evening comes, do not expect the morning; when morning comes, do not expect the evening. Take from your health for your illness, and from your life for your death.” Scholars explain that this is an encouragement to use each moment. It should not be understood as neglecting lawful work and responsibilities: the traveller still prepares for his road.
l: Travel light: ask of every possession, will this help me on the road?
Do not postpone repentance and good deeds.
Use your health and free time for what will remain.

en: On the authority of Ibn ‘Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took me by the shoulder and said: “Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a traveller.” And Ibn ‘Umar used to say: “When evening comes, do not wait for the morning; and when morning comes, do not wait for the evening. Take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death.”

ar: عَنْ أَبِي مُحَمَّدٍ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرِو بْنِ الْعَاصِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا، قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم «لَا يُؤْمِنُ أَحَدُكُمْ حَتَّى يَكُونَ هَوَاهُ تَبَعًا لِمَا جِئْتُ بِهِ».

s: An-Nawawi cites this as hasan sahih, narrated in Kitab al-Hujjah by ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As. Other scholars of hadith, including Ibn Rajab, have said that its chain is weak. Its meaning, however, is firmly supported by the Qur’an, which is why it is included and explained by the scholars.
m: “None of you truly believes until his desires (hawa) follow what I have brought.” The word hawa is the inclination of the self, its wants and likes. The test of faith is not what a person says but where his wants end up when truth and desire meet. The Qur’an says, “But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you the judge concerning what has arisen between them and then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have judged and submit in full submission” (4:65).

Scholars say that this is not about the absence of desires, since every human has them, but about their direction: that they come to love what Allah loves, and to dislike what He dislikes. It is the final stage of submission: the heart’s own preference falls in line.
l: Ask yourself in a decision whether you are looking for the ruling that suits you, or for what is right.
Train your wants gently: love what He loves, with du‘a and practice.
Make du‘a: “O Allah, make me love what You love.”

en: On the authority of Abu Muhammad ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “None of you truly believes until his desires follow what I have brought.”

ar: عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: سَمِعْت رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم يَقُولُ: قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى: يَا ابْنَ آدَمَ! إِنَّكَ مَا دَعَوْتنِي وَرَجَوْتنِي غَفَرْتُ لَك عَلَى مَا كَانَ مِنْك وَلَا أُبَالِي، يَا ابْنَ آدَمَ! لَوْ بَلَغَتْ ذُنُوبُك عَنَانَ السَّمَاءِ ثُمَّ اسْتَغْفَرْتنِي غَفَرْتُ لَك، يَا ابْنَ آدَمَ! إنَّك لَوْ أتَيْتنِي بِقُرَابِ الْأَرْضِ خَطَايَا ثُمَّ لَقِيتنِي لَا تُشْرِكُ بِي شَيْئًا لَأَتَيْتُك بِقُرَابِهَا مَغْفِرَةً.

s: At-Tirmidhi reports this from Anas ibn Malik and grades it hasan. an-Nawawi ends his collection with it as a sign of hope. The reader finishes the forty with Allah’s own words about forgiveness.
m: It is a hadith qudsi with three parts. “O son of Adam, as long as you call on Me and hope in Me, I forgive you what you have done, and I do not mind.” Two conditions: calling on Him and hoping in Him. “O son of Adam, even if your sins reached the clouds of the sky, then you asked My forgiveness, I would forgive you.” And the last: “O son of Adam, if you came to Me with an earth-full of sins and met Me without associating anything with Me, I would come to you with an earth-full of forgiveness.”

The only condition that is not negotiable in the hadith is tawhid: to die without having associated anyone with Allah. Short of that, the door is open. The scholars note the sequence of the hadith: du‘a and hope, then istighfar, then tawhid. They are the three keys of forgiveness.
l: When you feel the weight of your sins, return to this hadith and then raise your hands.
Do not let any sin make you stop calling.
Hold tightly to tawhid. It is the condition of everything.

en: On the authority of Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: Allah the Exalted said: “O son of Adam, as long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I forgive you for what you have done, and I do not mind. O son of Adam, if your sins reached the clouds of the sky and then you asked My forgiveness, I would forgive you. O son of Adam, if you came to Me with sins nearly as great as the earth and then met Me without associating anything with Me, I would come to you with forgiveness nearly as great as it.”
